body.heading: Presence is the whole job
paragraphs: When someone is sad, the instinct is to say something that lifts the cloud. But sadness is not a puzzle with a sentence-shaped key. What actually helps is duller and greater: your unhurried presence, a chair pulled close, a drink made without being asked.
You are not failing because the sadness stays. It was never yours to remove.

body.heading: A few sentences that hold up
paragraphs: Simple lines carry weight because they make no demands: “I’m here.” “You don’t have to talk.” “I’m not going anywhere.” Avoid ranking their loss (“At least…”) or borrowing it (“I know exactly how you feel”) — both move the spotlight off the person it belongs to.
If you do not know what to say, saying exactly that — “I don’t know what to say, but I’m here” — is honest, and honesty is comfortable to sit beside.

body.heading: The days after matter more
paragraphs: Support floods in during a crisis and evaporates by the following week, which is when ordinary life makes its unreasonable demands again. The message sent on a plain Tuesday — “Still thinking of you” — often lands deeper than anything said at the height of events.
Put a reminder in your calendar if you need to. Remembering later is not less sincere for having been scheduled; it is more reliable.

takeaway: Stay, keep your sentences simple, and remember to return on an ordinary day.
